original_question: Let Pi(n) be the product of the decimal digits of n and let Pm(n) be the first iterate count at which repeated application of Pi stabilizes. Is it true that every natural number n has multiplicative persistence at most 11, that is, Pm(n) <= 11?
correct_elements: Your draft is already aimed at the right problem: it uses the decimal digit-product map, asks about the stabilization time under iteration, quantifies over all natural numbers, and states the same conjectured universal upper bound 11 that appears in the paper.
missing_details: The paper works explicitly in base 10: Π(n) is the product of the digits in the usual decimal expansion of n.
The iterates are defined explicitly by Π^0 = Id and Π^k(n) = Π(Π^(k-1)(n)) for k >= 1.
Pm(n) is defined as the least positive integer k such that Π^k(n) = Π^(k+1)(n); this should be stated exactly rather than only saying 'when repeated application stabilizes.'
The positivity of the index matters: under the paper's convention, a one-digit number has Pm(n) = 1, not 0.
To be fully stand-alone, it is best to say that the decimal expansion is the usual one, i.e. without leading zeros.
The scope should remain exactly the paper's decimal multiplicative-persistence conjecture, without broadening to other bases or other persistence variants.
refined_question: In base 10, let Π: N -> N be the map that sends a natural number n to the product of the digits in its usual decimal expansion. Define the iterates by Π^0 = Id and Π^k(n) = Π(Π^(k-1)(n)) for k >= 1, and let Pm(n) be the least positive integer k such that Π^k(n) = Π^(k+1)(n). Is it true that Pm(n) <= 11 for every n in N?
justification: The draft clearly matches Gasull's Section 8 problem on multiplicative persistence, not any earlier conjecture in the paper. Problem 31 states exactly this decimal digit-product iteration question, introduces the iterate notation Π^k and the stopping-time notation Pm(n), and asks whether the universal bound 11 holds for all n in N. The immediately following discussion gives examples and a reduction-of-interest to numbers whose first iterate has prime factors among 2, 3, 5, 7, but that reduction is contextual and not a replacement for the conjecture itself.
